strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation addressing the practical tension between anytime-validity and deadline-constrained efficiency in sequential testing

Sound theoretical framework with interpretable results: Theorem 3.1 characterizes when Kelly betting is near-optimal in the 'on-schedule' interior region, while Propositions 3.4 and 3.6 provide sufficient conditions for aggressive/conservative betting
Intuitive phase diagram perspective (Figure 2) that clearly illustrates how optimal policies shift with problem difficulty and remaining time/gap
Principled progression from theory to practical methods: ϵ-greedy heuristics to DQN learning, well-motivated for handling unknown distributions
Comprehensive experimental setup with multiple baselines, oracle phase diagrams, detailed implementation documentation, and reproducibility support (extensive appendices, hyperparameters)
Correct mathematical development: proofs properly employ martingale concentration and large-deviations arguments (Sanov's theorem for finite support)
weaknesses: Severe limitation in experimental scope: all experiments use only Beta/Beta-mixture distributions, with N ≤ 200. Authors acknowledge this but provide no evidence the DQN generalizes to other families or realistic-scale A/B tests (N ~ 10,000+)

Theory restricted to finite-support distributions (Propositions 3.4 and 3.6), limiting generality. Conditions in Theorem 3.1 (√T log T ≲ ∆ ≲ ρϵT) are difficult to verify without knowing the true distribution in practice

Gap between theory and practice not adequately bridged: theory assumes known distribution to compute Kelly bets and rate functions I±, but impact of estimation error in empirical Kelly estimates λ̂t(m) on theoretical guarantees is unanalyzed. Early-time conservatism in DQN lacks theoretical justification
DQN training is expensive (500K episodes, 3 hours on L40s GPU) and only on synthetic Beta/Beta-mixtures. Generalization to other distributions untested; retraining required for new regimes

Modest empirical improvements over simpler baselines: hedged ϵ-schedules often competitive with DQN (Figure 3); confidence interval improvements ~15-20% (Figure 4). Statistical significance not formally tested. Unclear if gains justify added complexity
No real-world validation despite motivating applications (A/B tests, adaptive experimentation). All experiments are on synthetic data from restricted distribution families

Conditions in Propositions 3.4 and 3.6 are only sufficient, not necessary. Conservative correction terms c±T = O(log T/T) may dominate for practical finite T, limiting applicability. Examples suppress these terms only for intuition

Feature engineering for DQN (22-dimensional vector) appears ad-hoc with no ablation studies. DQN validation performance plateaus at ~0.55 hit rate (Figure 6), raising questions about optimality or fundamental limits

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: The paper elegantly articulates the tension between fixed-sample-size tests and fully time-uniform procedures, addressing a genuine need in A/B testing and adaptive experimentation with hard deadlines.

Insightful theoretical phase diagram analysis: Theorem 3.1 rigorously characterizes conditions where Kelly betting is near-optimal in interior regions, while Propositions 3.4 and 3.6 elegantly identify when aggressive/defensive betting outperforms Kelly using KL divergence rates.

Automatic anytime-validity by construction: The learned policy depends only on predictable features and respects betting constraints by design, ensuring anytime-validity without explicit enforcement—an elegant theoretical guarantee.

Thoughtful algorithm design: The 3-action discrete action set matches theoretical regimes, the 22-dimensional predictable feature vector enables distribution-sensitive adaptation, and universal training across randomized horizons/nulls/distributions is practical and novel.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple distribution families (Beta, Beta-mixture, Bernoulli), real data transfer without retraining (DNA methylation and relative humidity), extensive ablations, out-of-distribution generalization (logit-normal), and Type-I error verification.
Clear presentation with excellent visualizations: The phase diagram (Figure 1), rejection curves with learned action maps (Figure 3), and trajectory-level plots effectively communicate key insights.
weaknesses: Partial theoretical characterization: Theorem 3.1 only characterizes interior regions; Propositions 3.4 and 3.6 provide sufficient but potentially loose conditions. No minimax optimality results, lower bounds, or rigorous treatment of the regime boundaries and transitions.

Critical theory-practice gap: Theoretical results assume knowledge of PX (true Lmax, B, ε), yet the oracle phase diagrams require solving the DP with unknown PX. The paper provides no formal analysis of how empirical/estimated parameters affect optimality guarantees or whether the learned DQN policy respects theoretical predictions.

Restrictive scope of theoretical results: Theorem 3.1 and Propositions 3.4, 3.6 require finite alphabets; conditions in Eqs. (3) and (5) involve problem-dependent constants (ε, BK) with unclear general applicability. Theorems don't extend obviously to continuous distributions.

Modest empirical improvements with limited statistical rigor: Power improvements over STaR-Bets are 5–10% (visual estimates only; no confidence intervals or hypothesis tests). Real-data results: DQN is best in 5/6 cases but 'very close' in one—statistical significance unclear. No comparison with non-betting sequential testing frameworks.

DQN feature engineering and design choices under-justified: 22-dimensional feature vector includes heuristic components (skewness, excess kurtosis, Beta concentration proxy) with no ablation on importance. Why 3 actions? Limited training (550K episodes, ~3 hours) with no learning curve analysis. Generalization tested only on logit-normal, not broader distribution families.

Significant theory-practice gap in applicability: The connection between 'theory shows Kelly is near-optimal in interior regions' and 'train a DQN policy' lacks formal justification. No analysis of whether the learned policy respects or violates theoretical phase diagram structure, or how prediction errors in feature estimation affect performance.

Real-data experiments use resampling with replacement, sidestepping genuine non-i.i.d. challenges: This design choice reduces the practical relevance of transfer claims. No evaluation on truly streaming/sequential data.

Limited novelty in core methodology: The betting framework and e-processes are from prior work (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas, 2024). The main contributions are (i) finite-horizon analysis of the phase diagram and (ii) applying standard Deep Q-Learning. The Bellman recursion is standard DP.

strengths: Novel finite-horizon optimal control formulation: The casting of horizon-aware betting as a dynamic program over (t, log W_t) is original and yields valuable theoretical insights about when different betting strategies are optimal

Rigorous theoretical results: Theorem 3.1 provides concrete conditions under which Kelly betting is provably near-optimal in interior regions; Propositions 3.4-3.6 characterize aggressive and defensive regimes using KL-divergence rate functions

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive evaluation on synthetic (Beta/Beta-mixture/Bernoulli), out-of-distribution (logit-normal), and real data (6 real datasets spanning two domains); Type-I error verification confirms anytime-validity by construction
Interpretable learned policy: DQN modal-action maps recover theoretical phase diagram structure without explicit programming, demonstrating the policy learned meaningful concepts
Strong practical performance: Consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines (STaR-Bets/Hoeffding) with generalization across horizons, null values, and data distributions
Principled design ensuring validity: Maintains anytime-validity through predictable action constraints without sacrificing empirical performance
weaknesses: Theory provides only sufficient conditions: Propositions 3.4-3.6 characterize when aggressive/defensive betting helps but don't fully characterize optimal strategies or provide necessity results
Theorem 3.1 requires knowledge of problem-dependent constants (L_max, ε): In practice these are estimated, and the theorem doesn't account for estimation uncertainty in empirical Kelly estimates

DQN generalization not fully characterized: Trained exclusively on Beta/Beta-mixture distributions; while out-of-distribution transfer shown, boundaries of generalization remain unexplored. Extended action space (Figure 15) shows no improvement—unclear if fundamental or training limitation

Reproducibility concerns: No code repository provided (critical for validating DQN results); discretization details for phase diagram computation missing; real data uses resampling with replacement, breaking i.i.d. assumption

Presentation density: The path from Section 3 (theory) to Section 4 (practice) is abrupt; connection between interior regime (Theorem 3.1) and boundary regimes (Propositions 3.4-3.6) could be more explicit
Limited analysis of failure modes: No discussion of when the learned policy underperforms or how it behaves in extreme regimes (very large/small N, very small α)
